etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English store, stoure, storre, from Anglo-Norman stor, estore, estorr, estoer, and Old French estour, estor, from Latin īnstaurō.

definitions.definition: A place where items may be accumulated or routinely kept.

quote.citation: 1936, Robert Frost, “The Vindictives”, in A Further Range:
quote.text: And his subjects wrung all they could wringOut of temple and palace and store.

quote.citation: 1922 February, James Joyce, “[13]”, in Ulysses, Paris: Shakespeare and Company, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: But there was an infinite store of mercy in those eyes, for him too a word of pardon even though he had erred and sinned and wandered.

quote.citation: 1943 November – 1944 February (date written; published 1945 August 17), George Orwell [pseudonym; Eric Arthur Blair], Animal Farm […], London: Secker & Warburg, published May 1962, →OCLC:
quote.text: By late summer a sufficient store of stone had accumulated, and then the building began […] , under the superintendence of the pigs.

quote.citation: 2006, Carolly Erickson, The Last Wife of Henry VIII:
quote.text: What surprised us all was how Will's lighthearted nature and constant store of good humor won over one of the great heiresses of King Henry's court, Anne Bourchier.

definitions.definition: (mainly North American) A place where items may be purchased; a shop.

quote.citation: 1899, Stephen Crane, chapter 1, in Twelve O'Clock:
quote.text: There was some laughter, and Roddle was left free to expand his ideas on the periodic visits of cowboys to the town. “Mason Rickets, he had ten big punkins a-sittin' in front of his store, an' them fellers from the Upside-down-F ranch shot 'em up  […] .”

quote.citation: 1948, Carey McWilliams, North from Mexico: The Spanish-Speaking People of The United States, J. B. Lippincott Company, page 75:
quote.text: In 1866 Colonel J. F. Meline noted that the rebozo had almost disappeared in Santa Fe and that hoop skirts, on sale in the stores, were being widely used.

definitions.definition: A great quantity or number; abundance.

quote.citation: 1609, William Shakespeare, “Sonnet 37”, in Shake-speares Sonnets. […], London: By G[eorge] Eld for T[homas] T[horpe] and are to be sold by William Aspley, →OCLC:
quote.text: I make my love engrafted to this store.

quote.citation: a. 1645, John Milton, “L’Allegro”, in Poems of Mr. John Milton, […], London:  […]  Ruth Raworth for Humphrey Mosely, […], published 1646, →OCLC:
quote.text: With store of Ladies, whose bright eiesRain influence, and judge the priseOf Wit, or Arms, while both contendTo win her Grace, whom all commend.

definitions.definition: A head of store cattle (feeder cattle to be sold to others for finishing); a store cattle beast.
(transitive) To keep (something) while not in use, generally in a place meant for that purpose.

quote.citation: 1963, Margery Allingham, chapter 1, in The China Governess: A Mystery, London: Chatto & Windus, →OCLC:
quote.text: The half-dozen pieces  […]  were painted white and carved with festoons of flowers, birds and cupids. To display them the walls had been tinted a vivid blue which had now faded, but the carpet, which had evidently been stored and recently relaid, retained its original turquoise.

quote.citation: 2024 January 10, Chris Gilson, “RAIL's famous five...”, in RAIL, number 1000, page 27:
quote.text: Following allocation to Toton on January 1 1996, it stayed there until transferral to Crewe in November 2000, before being stored at Eastleigh on December 17 the same year.

definitions.definition: Have the capacity and capability to contain.
(transitive, computing) To write (something) into memory or registers.
(transitive) To stock, to fill (a container, repository, etc.) with things.

quote.citation: 1911, James George Frazer, The Golden Bough, volume 8, page 244:
quote.text: I have eaten my fill, and had my pockets well stored.
